podcast.title: Creative Peak and Financial Success (1951)
podcast.body: Hank Williams reached his creative apex in 1951, consistently writing and releasing number-one hits. During this period, he earned $1,000 per show, which, adjusted for inflation, would be equivalent to $13,000 today. "En 1951 al canso supico creativo, no paró de escribir éxitos y tener número 1 [...] ganaba $1,000 por show, que sumador la inflación actual que valdrían a los $13,000."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Final Journey and Death (December 31, 1952)
podcast.body: On New Year's Eve 1952, Hank Williams canceled a show due to an ice storm and hired Charles Carr, a university student, to drive him in his Cadillac Series 62 to a concert in Canton, Ohio. During the journey, he complained of pain and was given an injection of morphine and analgesics, which he mixed with alcohol. He collapsed in the backseat after writing a song. Four hours later, in Oak Hill, West Virginia, Carr discovered Williams' hand was cold, revealing his death at age 29. "En la vispera del año nuevo de 1952, Hanke Williams canceló un espectáculo por una tormenta de hielo, y encargo a Charles Carr, un estudiante universitario, llevarle en su Cadillac series 62 a nuevo concierto en Canton, o hallo."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Life of Pain and Instability (1952)
podcast.body: The year 1952, his last year of life, was marked by constant pain and pressure despite his external popularity. His chronic back pain persisted despite multiple unsuccessful operations, leading him to self-medicate with large quantities of alcohol and analgesics. This combination made him highly unstable, causing his performances to be erratic, ranging from memorable when sober to deplorable or completely absent when intoxicated. "1952 fue su último año de vida, y pese a que de cara al exterior estaba en su mejor momento de popularidad, internamente vivía bajo un dolor y una presión constante."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: "The Drifting Cowboys" Band Name Origin
podcast.body: Hank Williams named his band "The Drifting Cowboys" out of his deep admiration for Western movies and the figure of the cowboy. The band members adopted full Western attire, and Williams himself always wore his characteristic cream suit and large cowboy hat. "Hank Williams amaba las películas de lo este y la figura del vaquero, por eso le puso a su nombre a su banda, los cuales vestían con toda la indumentaria de lo este, y él empezó a vestir siempre con su característico, traje crema y su gran sombrero de vaquero."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Band Instability Due to Alcoholism
podcast.body: Following the departure of his original band members for WWII, substitute musicians who joined The Drifting Cowboys rarely lasted more than a day, primarily due to Hank Williams' severe alcoholism. This addiction also led to his dismissal from radio station WSFA. "Los miembros institutos que entraban en la banda, no aguantaban más de un día debido al alcoholismo de Williams. Esa abicción le llevó a que la misora WSFA lo despidiera."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Birth and Early Life
podcast.body: Born Hiram King Williams on September 17, 1923, in Montolive, Alabama. His father, a veteran of the First World War, worked on the railways, leading the family to move frequently. When Hank was seven, his father suffered facial paralysis from a war accident and was admitted to a veterans' hospital for the rest of his life, leaving Hank to be raised by his mother. "en Montolive, a la Bama, el 17 de septiembre de 1923, nace Jirán King Williams, que pasara la historia como Hanck Williams."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Brutal Rawness and Self-Destruction
podcast.body: Hank Williams sang with a brutal rawness and lived completely on the margins of society, leading a self-destructive lifestyle. His coherent embrace of this path, which culminated in his early death, mirrored the spirit of many later punk artists, even preceding them in his rebellious ethos. "Hank Williams cantaba con una crudeza brutal, vivía al margen de todo y se autodestruyó con más coherencia que muchos panks que vinieron después."

srcs.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)

podcast.title: Cause of Death and Enduring Mystery
podcast.body: The autopsy determined that Hank Williams died from right ventricular insufficiency. However, despite this official finding, mystery and rumors regarding the exact circumstances of his death continue to persist. "La autopsía determinó que murió por insuficencia del ventrículo derecho, aunque el misterio y los rumores sobre su fallecimiento, aún persisten."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Definition of Country Music
podcast.body: Hank Williams offered a concise definition of country music, emphasizing its narrative core. "As Hank Williams said, country music is just a story set to music."

podcast.title: Dismissal from Grand Ole Opry and Divorce
podcast.body: Due to his ongoing problems with alcohol, Hank Williams was fired from the Grand Ole Opry. Concurrently, his wife, Audrey Sheppard, divorced him. "De vida a sus problemas con el alcohol les despidieron del gran olopri. Su mujer, Rodri S. Separ, se divorció de él."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Dropped by Grand Ole Opry for Drunkenness, Performed on Louisiana Hayride
podcast.body: Hank Williams was dropped by the top-tier Grand Ole Opry due to drunkenness but subsequently found a performing spot on the Louisiana Hayride, a show known for booking acts on their way up or down. "Hank Williams started performing on it when he was dropped by the Opry for drunkenness."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Radio Debut (WSFA)
podcast.body: In 1936, at just 13 years old, Hank Williams began playing his guitar and singing in front of the WSFA radio studios in Montgomery, Alabama. His talent quickly caught the attention of the station's producers, who invited him to perform on a program. Due to the constant listener requests, he was hired by the radio station and subsequently formed The Drifting Cowboys. "En 1936, con tan solo 13 años, empezó a tocar su guitarra si el Burton frente a los estudios de radio VW S.F.A. el Montgomery a la Bama."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Family Connection to Sonny Jones
podcast.body: Hank Williams' widow was the sister of local guitarist Sonny Jones, who played a significant role in helping Dale Hawkins establish his first band. "Jones had a lot of contacts in the local music industry and how Hawkins pulled together the first line-up of his band when he was 19."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 63: "Susie Q", by Dale Hawkins

podcast.title: First Guitar and Mentorship
podcast.body: At the age of eight, Hank Williams' mother gave him his first guitar. He spent most of his days playing it on the street, where he met Rufus "Tee Tot" Payne, an African-American Blues musician. Payne showed Williams that music extended beyond sheet music, focusing on lived experience and feeling, and taught him the importance of honesty and an unshakeable rhythm, which became foundational to his style. "se crió con su madre, que el de regaló su primera guitarra cuando tenía 8 años."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Honky Tonk Performances and Alcohol Consumption
podcast.body: During his tours through the Southern United States, Hank Williams frequently performed in honky tonks, which were rustic bars typical of the region. According to his biographers, he spent a significant portion of his show earnings on alcohol consumed in these venues, marking the beginning of his severe drinking problem. "Cuando esos conciertos donde Hank empezó a consumir grandes cantidades de alcohol, según relató sus biografías, gastaba a gran parte de los ingresos del espectáculo en beber en esos locales."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Influence from Rufus T. Tott Paine
podcast.body: Hank Williams was significantly influenced and taught how to play guitar chords by the African American street musician, Rufus T. Tott Paine. Paine also taught Williams how to blend blues elements into country western music, highlighting the biracial roots of the genre. "Hank Williams was influenced, taught how to play guitar chords and blend blues into country western by the African American street musician, Rufus T. Tott Paine."

podcast.title: Influence on Kid Rock's Vision
podcast.body: Hank Williams was cited by Kid Rock as an influence on his musical vision, which he described as "very white trash Public Enemy style rap, plus The Stooges, plus Kiss, plus Hank Williams," also noting Kid Rock's admiration for country music. "A vision he calls very white trash public enemy style rap, plus the stooge's plus kiss plus Hank Williams. Like I said, he's a big country fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lifelong Favorite of Thomas Hicks
podcast.body: The music of Hank Williams became a favorite of Thomas Hicks (later Tommy Steele) for the rest of his life after Hicks fell in love with it on an early trip with the merchant navy to America. "he fell in love with the music of Hank Williams, who would remain a favorite of his for the rest of his life."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 48: "Rock With the Caveman" by Tommy Steele

podcast.title: Liked by Janice Martin for "Rock" Influence
podcast.body: Janice Martin appreciated Hank Williams' music, particularly the "little rock" element she found in his honky-tonk sound, contrasting with her general dislike for slower country ballads and bluegrass. "She liked Hank Williams because he had a little rock to his music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Limited Musical Education
podcast.body: Hank Williams never learned to read or interpret music, with his encounter with Rufus "Tee Tot" Payne being virtually his only formal musical training. Despite this, he composed some of the genre's most honest and emblematic songs. "Prácticamente, esta fue la única formación que tuvo en su carrera, ya que nunca aprendió a leer ni interpretar música."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Marriage to Audrey Sheppard and Son's Birth
podcast.body: During a hiatus in his career after being fired from WSFA and while the war ended, Hank Williams married Audrey Sheppard. They had a son, Randall Hank Williams, who later became known as Hank Williams Jr. and pursued a respected career in country music. "Y aquí tenemos un parón de unos años en su carrera, en los cuales se vivió a otras tareas, y se casó con Audrey Sheppard, con quien tuvo un hijo Randall Hanck Williams, que en años después de la muerte de su padre, se ha conocido como Hanck Williams Jr., y tendrá una respetada carrera en el country."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Obsession by Young Dylan
podcast.body: Shortly after his infatuation with Johnny Ray's music, young Robert Zimmerman (Bob Dylan) became deeply drawn to Hank Williams' music and obsessed with his songwriting. "he fell for the music of Hank Williams at a big way, and became obsessed with Williams' songwriting."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Paul Gilly Ghostwriting Claim
podcast.body: Some sources, primarily a self-published book, claim that Paul Gilly secretly ghostwrote several of Hank Williams's hits, including "Cold Cold Heart" and "I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry." "who is also considered by some to have secretly ghostwritten a number of Hank Williams' hits, including Cold Cold Heart and I am so long so might could cry."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Posthumous Legacy and Influence
podcast.body: Following his death, Hank Williams became a legend, with musicians like Elvis Presley, The Rolling Stones, and Bob Dylan not only covering his songs but also recognizing him as a pivotal figure in popular music. He is credited with ushering Country into the modern era and expanding its reach across the continent, akin to Camarón de la Isla's impact on Flamenco. "Tras su muerte, el cowboy que le había cantado al pueblo americano se convirtió en leyenda, fue al referente diiónicais y músicos de la talla del Vistrezley, los Rolling Stones o Bob Dylan no solo le versionaron, sino que lo reconocieron como una figura clave dentro de la música popular."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Second Marriage to Billie Jean Jones and Health Decline
podcast.body: Shortly after his divorce from Audrey Sheppard, Hank Williams married Billie Jean Jones. Towards the end of 1952, he began to suffer from cardiac problems, adding to his existing health struggles. "al poco se casó con Belijín Jones. A finales de ese año, empezó a sufrir problemas cardíacos."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Spina Bifida Occulta and Addiction
podcast.body: Hank Williams was born with spina bifida occulta, a spinal disorder that caused him intense pain throughout his life. This condition was identified as the primary reason for his later addiction to alcohol and drugs. "Nació con espina bifida oculta, un trastorno de la columna vertebral, el cual le causó intensos dolores durante el resto de su vida, y fue el principal motivo de eso futura adicción al alcohol y las drogas."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: The "Shakespeare of the Hillbillies"
podcast.body: Hank Williams was dubbed the "Shakespeare of the Hillbillies" for his brutally honest songs, written in the everyday language of the common man. His unique lyrics and bluesy phrasing set him apart. "Se empezaron a llamar el Seexpyr Gilbilly [...] Sus letras y sus fraseos, las timeros y bluseros eran únicos."

srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: World War II Disqualification
podcast.body: On December 7, 1941, the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor led to the United States' entry into World War II, resulting in his entire band being called to serve. However, Hank Williams himself was medically disqualified due to injuries sustained from falling off a bull in a rodeo in Texas. "El 7 de diciembre de ese año, la armada imperial japonesa atacó per Harbour, lo que llevó a Estados Unidos a entrar oficialmente en la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Toda su banda fue llamada a finlas, sin embargo, él fue descalificado médicamente debido a las igualas que tuvo en un accidente al caerse de un toro en un rodeo en Texas."
